claim.text: Under the specific iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) regime adopted for Trojan analysis — where after each pruning round the surviving weights are not rewound to their initialization and all finetuning uses only the potentially poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$ (no clean data) — the Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ (as defined in note 1) is approximately zero for non-Trojan (clean) models.

A significantly positive peak in the Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ (as defined in note 1) along the IMP pruning path indicates an atypical pruning stability fingerprint associated with a backdoor.

Computing the Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ (as defined in note 1) along the IMP pruning path yields a data-free detector that identifies pruning levels where Trojan information is isolated.

Empirically, across multiple architectures and datasets and for diverse Trojan types, there exists an extreme-sparsity subnetwork—termed the winning Trojan ticket—identified by a peak in the Trojan score (the LMC-based metric $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ that quantifies pruning-induced stability via the error barrier between un-finetuned and finetuned Trojan tickets), which simultaneously (i) preserves the Trojan attack effectiveness in terms of attack success rate (ASR) nearly as well as the original dense Trojan model and (ii) has near-random standard accuracy (SA) on clean inputs due to the aggressive pruning.
For example, for ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10 with an RGB trigger, at very extreme sparsity the winning Trojan ticket exhibited ASR = 94.49% while SA dropped to 11.38%.
Across experiments, winning-ticket ASR values reached 99.6% for RGB triggers and 99.8% for clean-label triggers.

The winning Trojan ticket (the extreme-sparsity subnetwork identified by a peak in the Trojan score) is consistently associated with the peak Trojan score (the LMC-based metric $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ that quantifies pruning-induced stability via the error barrier between un-finetuned and finetuned Trojan tickets) along IMP.

Using the winning Trojan ticket as the victim model in a trigger-recovery optimization $$ \min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n,\;\delta}\; \mathbb{E}_x\big[\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}(x'(z,\delta);\phi,t)\big] + \gamma\,h(z,\delta), $$ with $x'(z,\delta)=(1-z)\odot x + z\odot\delta$, C\&W targeted loss $\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}$, and the regularizer $h$ from prior work, and solving the label-wise optimizations followed by selecting the label with minimum $\|z^*\odot\delta^*\|_1$, recovers the correct Trojan target label more reliably than applying the same optimization to the dense model.

Using the winning Trojan ticket as the victim model in a trigger-recovery optimization $$ \min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n,\;\delta}\; \mathbb{E}_x\big[\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}(x'(z,\delta);\phi,t)\big] + \gamma\,h(z,\delta), $$ with $x'(z,\delta)=(1-z)\odot x + z\odot\delta$, C\&W targeted loss $\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}$, and the regularizer $h$ from prior work, and solving the label-wise optimizations followed by selecting the label with minimum $\|z^*\odot\delta^*\|_1$, recovers a trigger that, when stamped onto test images, achieves substantially higher ASR.
on ResNet-20s, CIFAR-10, (a) gray-scale trigger: recovered ASR = 91.2% (winning ticket) vs 71.4% (dense baseline);
The recovered triggers from winning Trojan tickets are effective even when the recovery optimization uses only 100 Gaussian noise images as base inputs rather than any clean images.

Empirically, across the four architectures ResNet-20s, ResNet-18, VGG-16, and DenseNet-100 and the three datasets CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Restricted ImageNet and for the four Trojan types gray-scale patch, RGB patch, clean-label, and stealthier WaNet, there exists an extreme-sparsity subnetwork—termed the winning Trojan ticket—identified by a peak in the Trojan score (the LMC-based metric $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ that quantifies pruning-induced stability via the error barrier between un-finetuned and finetuned Trojan tickets), which simultaneously (i) preserves the Trojan attack effectiveness in terms of attack success rate (ASR) nearly as well as the original dense Trojan model and (ii) has near-random standard accuracy (SA) on clean inputs due to the aggressive pruning.

note.text: elaboration of Trojan score: the Trojan score is defined to quantify the pruning-induced stability of Trojan tickets by measuring the linear-mode connectivity (LMC) error barrier between the un-finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta)$ and the $k$-step finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$.
